I'll think this through as the farmer.

**My reasoning:**

I farm 220 mu here in Quzhou — that's a big operation for our area, and because I finished school beyond middle school I try to plan it properly instead of just copying my neighbors. Five years in, I have a feel for what this soil does. The ground here is typical North China Plain loam, decent but it needs fertilizer to really produce. I split my land between millet (谷子) and spring soybean because rotation keeps the soybean disease down and the soybean residue helps the millet the next cycle. I'll put roughly half into each — 110 mu millet, 110.1 mu soybean.

For millet, I'm planting 张杂谷 hybrid seed — my neighbor tried it two years back and got over 400 kg/mu, far better than the old traditional seed my father used. I'll go with about 10 kg N per mu as urea, 5 kg P2O5, and 5 kg K2O, mostly as a compound fertilizer (15-15-15, around 25 kg/mu) at sowing, then top-dress 8 kg urea at jointing. Millet tolerates drought but I have well water, so I'll irrigate twice — once before sowing to get moisture, once at heading. Two sprays: one for locusts/armyworm, one for粟灰螟. Rotary till is enough, the ground was soybean last cycle so it's loose. I'll aim for 350 kg/mu — realistic, not greedy.

For soybean, the plant fixes its own nitrogen so I only give a starter — 3 kg N per mu. But I will not skimp on phosphorus, that's where soybean yield comes from: 6 kg P2O5 and 5 kg K2O. Improved variety (中黄 series). Spring soybean here, I irrigate at flowering and podding — two times. Three pesticide sprays: aphids early, pod borer mid, and a fungicide at flowering because I'd rather spend 20 yuan a mu than lose pods. I'll plough the soybean ground deeper to break any pan. Target 200 kg/mu — I won't gamble on 250.

I'd rather spend a bit extra on fertilizer than short the crop. On 220 mu a 10% yield loss is far more money than a bag of urea.
